transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-06-02
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~78 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (SE), Samir Gupta (SE), Emily Carter (CTO, BlueHarbor), Miguel Santos (Lead ML), Rina Okafor (Platform), Tom Vasquez (SRE)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
- Deep dive on reserved GPU sizing, burst routing, queueing models and KV cache warmup strategies for BlueHarbor's on-prem and VPC needs.
- Agreed to run a 24h prewarm + burst benchmark and deliver runbook/draft sizing.
- Security and KMS/KV integration are blockers for on-prem pilot; Redwood to share SOC2 excerpts and KMS patterns.

Topics: reserved_pools, burst_policy, prewarm, kv_cache, batching, quantization, VPC_onprem, SOC2, KMS

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: hey everyone, uh thanks for joining. quick intros — i'm jordan from redwood, i'm the ae on this deal.
[00:07] Emily Carter: hey jordan, emily here. thanks. big agenda for us, we want to nail how reserved capacity and burst works with our on-prem footprint.
[00:15] Priya Nair: hi emily, priya here. i'll lead the technical portion — we'll walk through queueing models, kv cache warmup, and then get into evictions.
[00:24] Miguel Santos: cool, i'm miguel. our core worries are p95 under load and that cold-kv penalty when traffic spikes after downtime.
[00:33] Rina Okafor: and for us the networking piece matters — VPC peering, private control plane, and KMS/HSM routing.
[00:39] Samir Gupta: quick note — some terms we'll use: prewarm (pre-starting models/pools), reserved (committed GPU pool), burst (ephemeral extra capacity), kv (k v) cache repopulation.

[03:02] Jordan Lee: alright, high level first — blueharbor's stated SLOs? emily?
[03:08] Emily Carter: we're targeting p95 < 300ms for our small prompt flows and p99 < 900ms for larger documents. sustained throughput is moderate, but we see spikes up to 8x during checkout windows.
[03:23] Tom Vasquez: yeah those spikes are short — 5 to 12 minutes typically — so the economics of reserved vs burst are critical.

[06:10] Priya Nair: given that, two recommended patterns — first: keep a right-sized reserved pool sized for baseline plus short headroom, with prewarmed models and warmed KV caches. second: add burst pools that can be routed to with relaxed SLOs; route only non-critical or degrade quality (quantized models) during burst.
[06:34] Miguel Santos: when you say warmed KV caches, do you mean persistent local KV on GPUs or shared redis? we currently use remote redis in our VPC.
[06:40] Priya Nair: yeah great question. we support both. remote redis gives consistency but has higher cold miss latencies across cold starts. local KV caches on the serving nodes dramatically reduce token generation latency after warmup, but you need repopulation strategies.

[09:12] Samir Gupta: a common approach is incremental repopulation: prefix caching first, then full kv fill in the background. for short spikes pre-populating top-k prefixes (we call it top-n warm) buys the p95.
[09:28] Rina Okafor: how do we do top-n warm practically? we dont have a perfect list of prefixes; traffic is varied.
[09:34] Priya Nair: we can use a sampled distribution from your production traces (top 1k prefixes) and simulate. that was mentioned in our onboarding doc — we'll ask for 7 days of traces.

[12:00] Miguel Santos: can we talk queueing model? we've been testing with a naive queue and see tail latency blow up.
[12:08] Priya Nair: yep, two useful models — M/M/c is a starting point for poisson arrivals and exponential service. for real workloads G/G/1 or an empirical distribution is better; the core output is utilization (rho). when rho > 0.7 you start seeing p99 cliffs.
[12:33] Samir Gupta: important to factor KV miss penalty into service time distribution. a miss can add 60–250ms depending on remote redis or local miss. that nonstationary tail distorts autoscaler behaviour.

[15:40] Jordan Lee: about autoscaler triggers — blueharbor prefers request-based concurrency threshold vs queue-length. any preference?
[15:47] Tom Vasquez: request-based sounds simple but we care about tail latency. queue-length gives you backlog signal but can be too late.
[15:55] Priya Nair: hybrid approach: use predictive headroom — short-term predictor of incoming qps (20–60s window) + queue-length as fallback. scale actions differ: prewarm described as background start without routing; warm-up complete flips route.

[19:11] Miguel Santos: ok, reserved sizing mechanics — do you size to 50th percentile traffic then let burst handle the rest?
[19:18] Priya Nair: we usually recommend baseline = p50 sustained qps or token rate + 10–20% safety margin. reserved handles steady-state plus low-level variance; burst handles spikes. reserved pools are cheaper per-token, and also a place where KV stays hot.
[19:36] Jordan Lee: also note reserved pools can be pinned to model versions so you avoid degradation during rollouts.

[22:05] Rina Okafor: on the private/on-prem side: control plane placement — do we run the control plane on-prem or do you offer a private control plane in our VPC?
[22:12] Samir Gupta: both options — private control plane in your VPC is common; fully on-prem airgapped is possible but requires extra ops. for KMS we integrate with customer KMS/HSM via our connectors; you keep keys.
[22:30] Emily Carter: security is a blocker. we need SOC2 artifacts and a KMS playbook before pilot.
[22:36] Jordan Lee: yeah we'll share SOC2 excerpt and our private deployment checklist. also outline SSO (SAML) and RBAC options.

[25:05] Priya Nair: back to latency — quantization tradeoffs during burst: you can fall back to 8-bit quantized variants on burst pools to cut GPU memory and increase capacity. quality drop is small for some workloads but test required.
[25:24] Miguel Santos: we saw hallucinations go up slightly with aggressive quant, so we may route low-risk flows to quantized models only.

[28:48] Samir Gupta: eviction policy when reserved pools need room: we support prioritized fairness. lower-priority routes get preempted; we also support soft-eviction where requests are drained first. important to have route-level priorities mapped to SLO tiers.
[29:07] Tom Vasquez: and what about preemptible instances? do you recommend them for burst?
[29:14] Priya Nair: preemptible is cheaper but riskier for long generated sequences. good for short stateless requests if you accept retries. otherwise prefer ephemeral but reserved-backed burst nodes.

[32:00] Miguel Santos: i'd like to see numbers: e.g. if baseline reserved = 8 GPUs, burst adds up to 24 more for 10 minutes, what's the warmup penalty?
[32:09] Jordan Lee: depends on model and KV strategy. for a 7B dense model with local KV warm, prewarm time ~30–50s to reach steady token throughput; full KV repopulation could take several minutes. that's why top-n warm is critical.
[32:30] Priya Nair: also consider batching behavior — continuous batching increases throughput but also increases median latency slightly. if you configure max latency budget for batching you can tune throughput vs latency.

[35:41] Rina Okafor: network egress inside on-prem is minimal but peering to our central redis will add 25–80ms depending on path. is there a hybrid cache option?
[35:50] Samir Gupta: yes, hybrid: local L1 KV with background reconciliation to remote redis. L1 misses hit remote redis and then populate L1. that reduces impact on token latency.

[38:12] Miguel Santos: for batching, what are best practices for adaptive batch windows during spikes?
[38:20] Priya Nair: adaptive batching that shortens windows under high QPS is typical. use a target max latency per request and let batcher cut windows accordingly. plus dynamic batch size caps per GPU to avoid OOM with quantized models.

[41:05] Jordan Lee: let's walk through a sample runbook flow for an upcoming sale spike (checkout) — Rina, imagine 9:55pm window next friday.
[41:13] Rina Okafor: yes.
[41:15] Priya Nair: runbook: 1) baseline reserved pool is warmed at T-20m, top-n prefix loading starts at T-15m, 2) predictive autoscaler arms at T-10m, 3) at T-5m prewarmed burst nodes are started but not routed, 4) upon QPS crossing threshold route to burst (with quantized fallback) and start background full-kv repopulation.
[41:42] Miguel Santos: and rollback if p95 exceeds 1s?
[41:45] Jordan Lee: yes, automatic fallback: demote to more conservative routing (send non-critical to quantized), or scale up reserved temporarily if capacity available, otherwise circuit-break nonessential flows.

[44:00] Tom Vasquez: how do we measure the cost delta? we need clear per-token cost assumptions for reserved vs burst vs preemptible.
[44:08] Jordan Lee: we'll provide an economics sheet — rough rule: reserved is X $/token lower than burst; preemptible is cheapest but variable. we'll run the benchmark and produce concrete numbers for your models.

[47:22] Rina Okafor: ON-PREM deployment specifics — HSM certs, firewall rules, control plane endpoints. any gotchas?
[47:30] Samir Gupta: main gotcha is time to fetch model artifacts and build kernels. pre-building container images and having model artifacts cached on local object store pre-deployment reduces first-time start by 40–60%. also GPU driver compatibility matters.

[50:05] Miguel Santos: long-lived KV state: if we do on-disk KV snapshots between restarts, can we restore quickly?
[50:11] Priya Nair: yes you can persist hot KV snapshots and rehydrate into local KV on boot. snapshot restore is faster than full replication but depends on snapshot size; we recommend incremental snapshots and delta patches.

[53:40] Emily Carter: one more question on compliance — is audit logging granular enough to show token-level request provenance?
[53:47] Jordan Lee: yes, we provide per-request trace ids, model version, route, and token counts in logs. for private deployments logs can be forwarded to your SIEM.

[57:02] Miguel Santos: let's surface risk: what if a burst causes cascading cold starts across other services?
[57:09] Priya Nair: mitigation: shard bursts by tenant/route, use circuit-breakers, and apply priority-based eviction. and simulation beforehand often reveals cascading failure modes.

[61:15] Rina Okafor: are there sample configs or an infra template we can use?
[61:21] Jordan Lee: yes — we'll share a terraform+helm template for private deployment and a sample autoscaler config with thresholds.

[64:40] Tom Vasquez: practical asks: we want a run of the benchmark with our traffic next week; what do you need?
[64:48] Priya Nair: need API keys to a sandbox, the production token/entry distributions (anonymized), and target SLOs. we'll run both hosted and private-sim runs.

[68:00] Miguel Santos: about the quantized model variants — do you support mixed precision for half the layers?
[68:07] Samir Gupta: we support multiple quant profiles: per-layer mixed precision, 8-bit, 4-bit (where hardware supports) and pruning-aware variants. quality regressions vary by model. we'll A/B test.

[72:12] Emily Carter: ok sounds good. want to confirm deliverables and owners.
[72:20] Jordan Lee: confirmed — run benchmark (redwood), runbook draft (redwood), traces from blueharbor, security docs (redwood). we'll sync on 6/9 for results.
[72:36] Miguel Santos: thanks — appreciate the technical depth.
[72:40] Jordan Lee: thanks everyone. we'll follow up with calendar invites and the artifact links.
